description: We're AstroGirls, a team of five women passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation! Several of us work at NASA, and we're bringing together our backgrounds in software engineering, data science, and space technology to tackle real-world challenges. We're excited to build something meaningful, learn from each other, and have fun along the way! 🚀✨
summary: Planetary Explorer is a web application designed to help researchers evaluate potential Mars landing sites, identify verified Earth analog environments, and develop detailed exploration missions. By entering mission parameters and adjusting interactive priority settings, researchers can dynamically rank candidate sites while exploring previously unstudied Earth terrain surveys. Each recommendation is supported by scientific data from over 95 verified data with metrics and calculations traceable to NASA, ESA, USGS, and peer-reviewed literature. Through transparent methodologies and evidence-based explanations, Planetary Explorer provides a reliable framework for developing informed research strategies that advance humanity's exploration of Mars.
details:
The Why Behind Planetary Explorer

We built Planetary Explorer for space researchers. Choosing where to land on Mars is a hard problem. The data is spread across many datasets and papers, and it takes a long time to compare sites by hand. We wanted one place where a researcher can describe a mission, see which sites fit it with Earth analogs, and check every number behind the answer.

What a researcher can do

A researcher starts by writing their mission in plain words. The app reads it and suggests priorities, such as gentle slopes, low elevation or strong sunlight. The researcher can adjust these with sliders and the rankings update right away. The app ranks 17 Mars sites and 17 paired Earth sites. The Earth sites matter because a mission can be tested on Earth before it flies. The app also surveys 144 less-studied Earth areas across 16 regions to find new test sites that researchers may not know about.

Built on NASA and ESA data

We did not want to guess anything, so the app is built on real space agency data.

Mars slope, relief and elevation are calculated from NASA's MOLA elevation data. Earth terrain comes from the Copernicus elevation model, which is part of the European programme that ESA helps run. Earth rainfall comes from NASA POWER. Gravity and pressure come from NASA fact sheets. Site photos come from NASA's image library and from NASA and ESA mission pages.

Mars and Earth terrain are compared at the same 3.7 km scale, so the comparison is fair. Every score runs from 0 to 100 and comes from fixed formulas. The language model only reads the mission and writes explanations. Fixed code checks its suggestions and calculates every score.

Research we can stand behind

The app cites 95 sources. 22 of them are NASA pages and datasets, and the rest are research papers and ESA pages. Site labels and mission findings are tied to 109 word-for-word quotes from those sources, so a researcher can see the exact sentence a claim comes from. When something has not been checked yet, the app says so. When data is missing, the app shows it as missing and never fills it in. While not all of the sources were inputted into the sources prompt on the project submission page, they can be all found on the webpage. 

This was the part we cared about most. A tool for researchers is only useful if they can trust it.

How this helps researchers develop Mars

We see Planetary Explorer as a starting point for real mission planning and two tabs already point that way. The Research tab turns a site into a research plan. It shows study ideas, the next investigations to run, the risks and missing evidence, and the sources behind each point. The Plan an Expedition tab lets a researcher lay out a rover route on orbital imagery of the site. The app then calculates the distance, energy use, slopes and whether the route is feasible.

Together, these let a researcher go from "which site?" to "what would we study there, and how would we get around?" Next, we plan to add Mars temperature, rock and dust data, and a full Moon globe, so the same tool can support lunar missions too.
